literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. The big news in the English-language book world is a Booker Prize winner who is a little unexpected, and around it there are some lovely pieces on music, art, and the sound of language itself.

Let's start with the Booker. M. John Harrison has won the twenty twenty-six prize for The End of Everything, announced at a ceremony in London. The Guardian reports that he is eighty-one, which makes him the oldest winner, and that he is the first science fiction author ever to take the prize. The novel is post-apocalyptic, set on a near-future Kent coast. Literary Hub says the judges describe a book that turns you upside down and raises a wry smile, and I rather like that as a recommendation. The BBC calls it "baffling but brilliant", which suggests a novel that doesn't hold your hand. I should say that for the BBC's report, and for its separate piece in which Harrison talks about the book, I only have the headlines, so I can't give you more than that. The Observer has the fullest piece on why it won, and that is where I'd begin if you want to understand the choice. And if you like to know what else was in the running, The Independent's critic read all six shortlisted novels and names the one to pick up. It's a handy guide to the shortlist, and perhaps to your own reading list.

Now to novels that tie together music, history and ideas, which I think are your sort of thing. The Guardian reviews Jonathan Coe's Lessons in Harmony, which imagines a friendship between Ravel and Ralph Vaughan Williams. The two composers are searching for a musical identity, and the book asks what music can tell us about national identity. It's a lovely premise: two great ears, one French and one English, listening for what their countries sound like. Given your love of classical music and of history learned through fiction, it seems made for you. The Guardian also reviews Two Women, Jacqueline Rose's second novel, which is a fictional biography. It alternates between chapters on her sister, the philosopher Gillian Rose, and chapters on another philosopher, Edith Stein. The reviewer calls it a memorial to Gillian, and it weaves together biography, memoir and philosophy. That sounds like a demanding but rewarding read.

For art and fiction together, Literary Hub has a conversation with Olivia Laing about her new novel, The Silver Book. It's set in the world of nineteen-seventies Italian cinema, and it deals with art, queer love and illusion. The piece praises her spellbinding prose, and I'd read it for the way she talks about building a world out of images, which is close to the paintings-and-literature territory you enjoy. It may also be useful to you in the classroom, as a way of talking about how a novelist can borrow the language of another art form.

On voices and worlds, there is a nice group today. BBC Radio 4's Open Book, broadcast today, has Becky Chambers talking about her new novel, As You Wake Break The Shell. It is the first of a duology, told in alternating timelines on a planet called Fortune. She speaks about building a planet from the ground up and about her Star Trek roots, and since she is known for warm, character-led science fiction, it should be a gentle listen. From Literary Hub there is also the opening of a piece, apparently from a novel, called This Impossible Life. It begins on the outskirts of Lagos, near the Third Mainland Bridge, where a character called Alohan has been dropped off by an old lady and wanders the roads astonished at his fate. The excerpt is cut off, but the voice and the situation look promising, and it's the sort of opening a student could step into without knowing Lagos at all. Also from Literary Hub, a short story called "Hello Daughter". Lori has not heard from her daughter Freddie for about a week and isn't sure of her current address. Their weekly exchange is a simple "hi", with the reply "I'm still not dead." It's a small piece with quietly sharp emotional force, and it might work well read aloud.

Something more lyrical now. Literary Hub has a reflection called "What It Means To Be a Basque Writer". It is about language, its beauty, and the grief of hearing one die out. It is written with real musicality, and I think you'll enjoy it for the sound of the sentences as much as for the subject. It may even stir thoughts about how many languages sit in your own classroom.

Finally, two pieces about the craft of writing. The Paris Review has made its archived Art of Biography interview with Robert Caro free to read. He talks about how a biography is built, and it's a rich read for anyone who loves a well-made narrative. They have also opened up a short story by Matthew Baker, "Why Visit America", so there's fiction and craft side by side. And Literary Hub has an appreciation of Janet Malcolm, written by someone who had been circling her work for years without quite realising it. It's an essay about a writer's style and about a reading life, which makes it good company for a quiet moment.

That's your literary morning, Yamuna. I hope something here finds its way into your bag, or onto the shelf by the window with the view of the valley.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. The big news in the books world today is a Booker Prize winner nobody could have easily predicted, and around it there are some lovely pieces on music, painting, language and the craft of writing.

Let me start with the prize, since it has filled the pages of nearly every outlet. M. John Harrison has won the twenty twenty-six Booker Prize for his novel The End of Everything. The announcement came at a ceremony in London. The Guardian adds a few details that make the story rather moving. Harrison is eighty-one, which makes him the oldest winner in the prize's history. And he is the first science fiction author ever to win. The novel is post-apocalyptic, and The Guardian places it on the coast of Kent in the near future. So we have an English seaside landscape, a world ending or already ended, and a writer who has spent a very long career working in a genre that prizes of this kind have tended to keep at arm's length. The Guardian calls the recognition well earned, and from what I can gather, most people seem to agree.

The BBC reports the win under a headline calling the book "baffling but brilliant", which is a fine thing to have said about your novel. That phrase tells you something about what kind of book this is. It is not a tidy, reassuring apocalypse. The judges, as quoted by Literary Hub, describe a book that turns you upside down and raises a wry smile. I rather like that combination. Disorientation and a wry smile suggest a narrator, or a narration, that is never entirely straightforward but is also not without humour. The BBC also has a separate piece in which Harrison talks about the book in his own words. I only have the headline for that one, so I can't tell you what he says, but it will be worth a look, because writers of his generation often say surprising things about their own work.

If you would like to understand the win rather than just hear about it, the Observer has what looks like the main analysis piece, asking why The End of Everything won. That is probably the best place to start if you read only one thing about the novel. And for anyone who likes to read shortlists as a kind of competition, The Independent's critic has read all six of the shortlisted novels and names the one to pick up. That is a useful guide to the shortlist as a whole, whatever you make of the outcome, and a good way to find a second Booker novel for the winter evenings.

Now, to something closer to your own taste for stories that teach history and thought. The Guardian reviews Jonathan Coe's new novel, Lessons in Harmony. It imagines a friendship between Maurice Ravel and Ralph Vaughan Williams, and follows the two composers in their search for a musical identity. The question the review poses is what music can tell us about national identity. It is a lovely premise: two composers, one French and one English, each trying to work out what it means to write music that belongs to a place without becoming merely local. It is also, I think, a rather good question for a bilingual, bicultural classroom like yours. A novel that explores national identity through sound and through friendship, rather than through politics, is a gentler and more interesting way into the subject. And given your love of classical music, I suspect you will enjoy the idea of Ravel and Vaughan Williams as characters, talking and arguing and listening to one another.

The Guardian also reviews Two Women, the second novel by Jacqueline Rose. It is described as a fictional biography, with alternating chapters on two figures: the author's sister, Gillian Rose, and the philosopher Edith Stein. The reviewer calls it a memorial to Gillian Rose. It weaves together biography, memoir and philosophy, which is a demanding mixture, but also the kind of book where form and feeling are tied closely together. A sister remembered alongside a philosopher: the structure itself suggests that grief and thought sit side by side. It is the sort of book that makes the line between a novel and an essay feel productively blurry.

Staying with art and illusion, Literary Hub has a conversation with Olivia Laing about her new novel, The Silver Book. It is set in the world of nineteen-seventies Italian cinema, and it is concerned with art, queer love and illusion. I'd normally keep you away from film-industry news, but this is a novelist talking about how she builds a world on the page, and the pairing of a visual art form with a writer's prose is exactly where your interests meet. Laing's prose is described as spellbinding, and a setting in which everything is staged and lit and framed gives a novelist plenty to work with when thinking about what is real and what is only beautiful.

From Italian cinema to an entirely invented planet. On BBC Radio 4's Open Book, broadcast today, the tenth of November, Becky Chambers talks about her new novel, As You Wake Break The Shell. It is the first book of a duology, told in alternating timelines on a planet called Fortune. She discusses the work of building a planet from nothing, and she talks about her Star Trek roots. That last detail is a charming one. Star Trek was always, at its best, about character and curiosity and how people of different kinds learn to live together, and Chambers is a writer who seems to carry that spirit into her fiction. The alternating timelines are also a structural device that you could talk about with your première students, because the way a writer interleaves two periods tells you a great deal about what they want the reader to put together for themselves.

Now a group of pieces about the craft itself. The Paris Review has made free from its archive the Art of Biography interview with Robert Caro, along with a short story by Matthew Baker called "Why Visit America". The Paris Review interviews are a wonderful form, long, patient conversations in which writers explain how they actually work. Caro on biography is a rich read for anyone who admires a well-built narrative, and it sits nicely alongside the other pieces today about how history and life are turned into stories.

Literary Hub also has an appreciation of Janet Malcolm's writing, titled The Enduring Genius of Janet Malcolm. It is written by someone who had been circling her work for a long time without quite realising it, and it is as much about a reading life as about a style. I find those essays particularly pleasing, because they show how a writer can get under your skin slowly, over years, before you notice it has happened.

And there is a piece I think you will especially enjoy for its music, called What It Means To Be a Basque Writer. It is a reflection centred on language, on its beauty, and on the grief of hearing one's language die out. It is described as lyrical and linguistic, and I think it will speak to your love of prose that has a musical quality. Living in the French Alps, in a bilingual school, you will have a particular sense of how a language carries a world inside it. A piece about a tongue that is fragile, and about writing in it anyway, seems a good one to read slowly.

Finally, two pieces of short fiction, both from Literary Hub, if you want something to read over a cup of tea. The first is a short story called "Hello Daughter". It follows a woman named Lori, who has not heard from her daughter Freddie in about a week and is not sure of her current address. Their weekly exchange, as described, is a simple "hi", and then a reply that says, "I'm still not dead." There is a quiet and rather sharp emotional charge in that small, dry exchange. It is the kind of detail that a good short story builds on: a whole relationship compressed into a few words, with love and distance and wry humour all present at once.

The second is an opening excerpt, apparently from a novel, titled This Impossible Life. It is set on the outskirts of Lagos, near the Third Mainland Bridge. A character called Alohan has been dropped off by an old lady and wanders the roads, astonished at his fate. The text I have is cut off, so I can't say where it goes, but the situation and the narrative voice look promising. A person set down in a place, with a sense of wonder and bewilderment, is a classic way into a story, and it is the kind of opening that makes you want to step in without needing to know the setting beforehand, which I know is a quality you value.

So, to gather it together: a prize for an apocalypse on the Kent coast, a pair of composers searching for a national voice, a sister remembered through philosophy, and a handful of pieces on how writers make their worlds. I hope one of them keeps you company on the way to the market this weekend.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. There's a pleasing thread of artists and their written voices running through the last couple of days, so let me start close to home and then wander out.

At the Musée de Grenoble, there's a date for your diary. On the twelfth and thirteenth of December, the actor Anne Castillo will perform readings from the journal of Anne Truitt, directed by Mathieu Barché. Truitt was a sculptor, so this is an artist's own written voice set among the museum's works, and I suspect it's exactly your sort of evening. Yesterday afternoon, the museum also hosted a talk for the Amis du musée, which screened and discussed Caroline Champetier's 2012 film on Berthe Morisot. That has passed now, but it's a reminder that the museum is running a good thread on painters' lives, and it may be worth watching for similar events.

Also in Grenoble, the Mois de la photo is under way. Le Dauphiné Libéré has published a guide to the events not to be missed, and a separate piece on two photographers offering what it calls two views of an unstable world. I only have the headlines, so I can't tell you which exhibitions or venues, but it sounds reflective and well worth a look in the paper. And l'Essentiel has asked a rather nice question: what history lies behind the walls of the Magasin-CNAC? It's a short piece, but if you've ever wondered about the story of that building, it's a good place to begin.

Now to a theme that I think will please you, which is André Malraux and his musée imaginaire. The Journal de Saône-et-Loire's site, jds.fr, carries two items on it. One is a route through Malraux and Picasso's idea of the imaginary museum, linking modern art with a man who was, of course, a novelist as well as a thinker about painting. The other is a series called "L'Art est une conquête", whose first season is devoted to the same subject. Both texts are very brief, so I can't say more than that, but the idea itself is a lovely one for a literature teacher: that a museum can exist in the mind, across pages and reproductions.

The Guardian, meanwhile, has been busy with Bloomsbury, and the pieces make a fascinating pair. Tate Britain is showing Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant, and the critic is unsparing. The review calls the show a flaccid roam through desperately mediocre modernists, and argues that the paintings are less compelling than the lives, the loves and the Picasso-filled home behind them. Set that beside a very different piece. Cordelia Roche remembers her father, the poet Paul Roche, and his thirty-year bond with Duncan Grant. Grant was friend and muse to him, but never lover. Her title gives the flavour: "My father loved Duncan more than he loved us". It's a personal, rather painful family story, and it brings the Bloomsbury world of painting and writing vividly to life. Read together, they ask a good classroom question: do we value this circle for its art, or for its stories?

On portraits and strong characters, there are three pieces. Beaux Arts Magazine has a quick two-minute profile of Séraphine Louis, known as Séraphine de Senlis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She was a self-taught pioneer of naïve art, famed for exuberant paintings, and her life story is a vivid one. The Guardian looks at Richard Avedon through Ron Howard's Netflix documentary, which follows his career as a photographer. It includes the lovely anecdote of the Dalai Lama laughing during a sitting, and it explores how Avedon hunted for faces that surprised him, trying to catch something of his sitters' inner selves. And the Guardian also reviews A Fox Under a Pink Moon, a film made from five years of smartphone footage of Soraya Akhlaghi, who fled Iran as a teenager. Her narration and her self-portrait make it a powerful character study, though the review makes clear it's a harrowing one, so perhaps one for a day when you're feeling robust.

For a bit of provocation, the Guardian also interviews the conceptual artist Ryan Gander, who is cheerfully bolshie. He says he dislikes painting and has scorn for the YBAs, the Young British Artists, and yet his new show is full of paintings. It's lively, and a good example of an artist's voice full of contradictions, which can be more revealing than any statement of principle.

If you fancy something to listen to, BBC Radio 4's Front Row Review Show looks at the stage version of The Lives of Others, directed by Robert Icke, which explores love and Stasi surveillance in East Germany. The same programme discusses the film La Bola Negra, based on a Spanish novel, and Tom McCarthy's new novel, The Rhyl Poster.

Finally, a little history brought to life. Twenty Minutes reports on an offbeat exhibition about William the Conqueror at the château de Falaise in Normandy, approached through a quirky angle on the Norman duke. The article is short, but the setting, in the castle of his birthplace, rather speaks for itself.

That's all for today, Yamuna, and I hope something here sends you off to a gallery or a good book.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art briefing begins close to home, in Grenoble, then wanders through Malraux's imaginary museum, the Bloomsbury circle, and a handful of lives told through portraits, journals and self-portraits.

Let me start in the city. The Musée de Grenoble has two things for you, one just past and one to put in the diary. Yesterday afternoon, Monday the ninth of November, at half past two, the Amis du musée held a talk built around Caroline Champetier's film on Berthe Morisot, made in twenty twelve. It has already happened, so I mention it mainly as a sign of the kind of programme the museum is running: a film that looks at how a life and a body of work can be told on screen, followed by discussion. If the museum repeats that sort of evening, it feels like one you'd enjoy.

The one to note is in December. On the twelfth and thirteenth, at the Musée de Grenoble, the actor Anne Castillo will perform readings from the journal of Anne Truitt, directed by Mathieu Barché. The event is called "Au fil des jours". Truitt was a sculptor, so this is an artist's own written voice set beside the museum's work, which suits your two loves of art and literature. There is something appealing about hearing a sculptor, who works in volume and silence, speak in the quiet daily register of a journal. It is one of those evenings where the language might matter as much as the objects. The twelfth is a Saturday, so it could fit a weekend trip down from Les Adrets.

Also local is a short piece from l'Essentiel asking what history lies behind the walls of the Magasin-CNAC. The Magasin is one of the city's key contemporary art venues, and the question is a nice one: a building that has had a life before and around its exhibitions. The text I have is only a short teaser, so I can't tell you the answer, but it may be worth a look if you like the story of a place as much as the art inside it.

And the Dauphiné Libéré is running two items on the Mois de la photo in Grenoble. One is a guide to the events not to be missed, the other is about two photographers offering, in its words, two views of an unstable world. I'm afraid only the headlines and a few lines are available, so I can't give you names or venues. But with the month under way, a reflective photography show with a sense of an unsettled world might make a good Saturday outing, perhaps paired with a stop at a market on the way.

Now to an idea that links painting and literature as neatly as anything. Two items from the Journal de Saint-Denis, jds.fr, point to André Malraux and the "musée imaginaire". One is a route through Malraux and Picasso's thinking on the idea, linking modern art with a man who was also a novelist. The other presents a series called "L'Art est une conquête", season one, devoted to the musée imaginaire. In both cases the text is very brief, little more than titles, so I can't describe what is on show. But the idea itself is a good one for a literature teacher to carry around. Malraux imagined a museum without walls, where works from anywhere and any age could sit side by side, which is not far from what you do in a classroom when a poem meets a painting. If you ever want a way into a lesson on how images and words talk to each other, that phrase alone is a good starting point.

Next, the Bloomsbury world, which this week is being looked at from two quite different angles in The Guardian. The first is warm and personal. Cordelia Roche remembers her father, the poet Paul Roche, and his thirty-year passion for the painter Duncan Grant. He was Grant's friend and muse, she says, but never his lover. The headline carries the heart of it: "My father loved Duncan more than he loved us." It is a family story, told by a daughter who grew up in a household shaped in the image of that circle, and it ties in with a major Grant exhibition. It is the sort of piece that gives you a narrator with a stake in the story, which is half of what makes any memoir work.

The second is a much cooler view. The Guardian's critic reviews the Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant show at Tate Britain, and the verdict is harsh. The headline calls it "a flaccid roam through Bloomsbury's desperately mediocre modernists". The argument is that the paintings are less compelling than the lives, the loves and the Picasso-filled home that lay behind them. You may or may not agree, but it's a useful counterpoint. It raises a question you could put to a class: when we read or look at work from a famous circle, how much of our interest is in the work, and how much in the gossip and the setting? Reading the daughter's tender memoir next to the critic's dismissal gives you two quite different Grants, one loved, one found wanting.

Let me turn to lives told through faces and images. The Guardian also looks at Richard Avedon, through Ron Howard's Netflix documentary on his career as a photographer. Avedon says he is "looking for faces which surprise me", and the piece uses anecdotes, such as the Dalai Lama laughing during a sitting, to show how he tried to capture the inner self of the people in front of his lens. For someone who enjoys the stories behind images, and how a portrait is as much a conversation as a likeness, it looks like a good read. It also sits well beside the Morisot film I mentioned: two ways of getting at a person, one with a camera in the studio, one with a camera trained on a painter's life.

Beaux Arts Magazine offers a quick profile of Séraphine Louis, known as Séraphine de Senlis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She is described as a pioneer of naïve art, with exuberant paintings, and a self-taught artist. It is only a two-minute read, but it is the kind of vivid life story that makes a character, and I think you'd enjoy it as a short, bright portrait of a woman who made her art on her own terms.

A much more harrowing self-portrait comes from The Guardian's review of "A Fox Under a Pink Moon". The film is built from five years of smartphone footage of Soraya Akhlaghi, who fled Iran as a teenager and was filmed through her precarious new life. The reviewer calls it a boldly imaginative self-portrait. What stands out for your interests is the narrator's own voice: she is both subject and storyteller, and the piece describes a strong character study. It is a hard watch, by the sound of it, so one to choose with care, but the idea of a young person shaping her own story from fragments of phone footage is striking, and it speaks to the way teenagers today record and narrate themselves.

For an artist's voice of a very different temper, there is a lively Guardian interview with the conceptual artist Ryan Gander. He is candid about disliking painting, and scornful of the YBAs, the Young British Artists, saying it was hard coming after what he calls their shallow, egocentric work. Yet his new show, as the piece points out, is full of paintings. The headline calls him "brilliantly bolshie", which gives you a sense of the tone. It's a good example of an artist whose contradictions are part of the pleasure, and it may make a fun read if you like hearing creators argue with themselves.

On the stage side of things, BBC Radio 4's Front Row had its Review Show this week. It covers the stage version of "The Lives of Others", directed by Robert Icke and starring Keira Knightley, which explores love and Stasi surveillance in East Germany. It also discusses "La Bola Negra", a Spanish film based on a novel, and Tom McCarthy's new novel, "The Rhyl Poster". It's the sort of programme that moves across media, from page to stage to screen, and the East German setting of the first has plenty of historical weight for anyone who likes to learn history through story.

Last, a small curiosity from Normandy. 20 Minutes reports on an unusual exhibition about William the Conqueror at the château de Falaise, approached through a quirky angle on the Norman duke. The article is brief and doesn't tell me much more than that, but history brought to life through objects and art, in the castle where the story began, is the kind of thing you might enjoy if you ever head that way. It also reminds us that the past is often best met on the spot, with a bit of imagination.

That's the round-up for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it finds its way into your week, perhaps a quiet hour with a journal, a photograph or a good argument about Bloomsbury.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet couple of days for official BFI texts, but there's a pleasing cluster of news around Hamlet, some stage versions of your set texts, and several oral-theme authors in the spotlight.

Let me begin with Hamlet, which dominates the day. Two outlets, Theatre Weekly and the London Evening Standard, have both published production images of a staging called Hamlet Hail to the Thief at the Barbican. The Standard bills its pictures as exclusive first photographs. Neither piece gives me dates or any detail beyond the images, so I can't tell you how the production treats the play. But Hamlet is on the session twenty twenty-seven programme, and a new London staging is worth watching as it develops. It could be a good springboard for asking première students how a production's visual choices shape their reading of the text.

Also on Hamlet, there's an article on the sentry's opening exchange, "Stand and unfold yourself", and how it may echo the royal court. It comes from a site called 白鲸出海, and all I have is the headline. Still, that first line is a lovely thing to take into class. It's a challenge shouted in the dark, from a guard who should be the one answering, and a close reading of it could open up the play's themes of watching, secrecy and who has the right to speak.

Staying with the 2027 set texts, there are two more productions to note, though again with little detail. Fairy Powered Productions has had a review published of its Great Expectations, and the University of Waterloo's Theatre and Performance department is presenting Twelfth Night. Neither item gives dates or specifics, so I can't say how faithful or inventive either one is. Separately, the University of Auckland has announced the return of its summer Shakespeare, this time a comedy double bill. I don't know which plays are involved, so I wouldn't promise a Twelfth Night connection, but it's a reminder of how widely these comedies are staged, and a nice detail to share with students who think Shakespeare belongs only to England.

On the practical side of teaching Shakespeare, Holy Cross Magazine has a piece on teaching the English language through Shakespeare. I only have the headline, but the idea suits your seconde and première classes well, where the language itself is as much the subject as the story.

Now to the oral themes, where Margaret Atwood features three times. First, Our Theatre Voice reviews the Canadian premiere of Alias Grace, the stage version of Atwood's novel based on a real nineteenth-century case. The reviewer praises compelling performances and restrained, subtle staging. That sounds well suited to a story built on ambiguity, where what's withheld matters as much as what's shown. It isn't one of your listed oral texts, but it's by the author of The Handmaid's Tale, and it might interest students who want to see how Atwood turns historical record into fiction.

Second, Creative Boom has a piece on the Balbusso Twins returning to The Handmaid's Tale. I only have the headline, so I can't say what their work looks like. But anything that brings illustration into conversation with the novel touches on your fondness for links between images and writing, and it might make a good visual prompt for the oral.

Third, Hotpress reports that Margaret Atwood, Sebastian Barry and Louise Kennedy are on the lineup for the Festival of Writing and Ideas in twenty twenty-seven. The report gives no dates or venue, so there's nothing to plan around yet. But it's good to know that Atwood is still appearing publicly, which is a nice thing to tell students preparing the oral.

Two more oral-theme authors appear. The University Times reports that the Irish novelist Paul Lynch, author of Prophet Song, is to visit The Phil, the Trinity College debating society in Dublin. No date is given. If recordings or write-ups follow, an author talking about his own novel is just the sort of material that can enrich an oral discussion. And Vocal has a tribute piece titled Celebrating Maya Angelou. Again I only have the headline, so I can't vouch for the content, but it concerns the author of I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, which is on your oral list.

Finally, three items from the wider literary world. The Booker Prize has gone to M. John Harrison for The End of Everything, a dystopian novel. LBC reports that at eighty-one he's the oldest winner, and the first science-fiction author to take the prize. It's a handy talking point for students of dystopian fiction. If your oral group is reading The Handmaid's Tale, Never Let Me Go or Parable of the Sower, you could ask whether the old line between genre fiction and literature still holds, and why a prize might change its mind.

Literary Hub asks the question of which literary TV adaptation is the best of all time. I only have the headline, but it's a fine debate to put to students: what does a screen version gain from a novel, and what does it lose? Adaptation is a good way into discussing narrators, and I suspect you'll have your own favourite.

And the Wall Street Journal looks at the reading list for what it calls the hottest class at Harvard. Again, just the headline, so I can't say what's on it. But seeing how a university frames its literature teaching can spark ideas for your own syllabus, perhaps as you look ahead to terminale.

That's the corner for today, and I hope the Barbican photographs offer a little theatre to brighten your morning.
bfi.long:

The piece is about what the line really means and how it might echo the royal court. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you how it argues the point. But the line itself is a fine thing to take into class. It's the play's very first demand for identity, spoken in the dark by someone who is nervous, and it quietly sets up a play full of people who will not unfold themselves. A short exercise on opening lines, asking what a play tells us before any king or prince appears, would suit seconde or première very well, and this article might give you a hook, provided you read it first to see whether you agree with it.

Staying with Shakespeare, there are two Twelfth Night items, both from universities, and both quite far from Grenoble. The University of Waterloo's Theatre and Performance department is presenting a production of Twelfth Night, and the University of Auckland has announced the return of its summer Shakespeare, a comedy double bill. Neither text gives dates or details, and I can't say whether the Auckland double bill includes Twelfth Night itself, so please take that one only as a general sign of a comedy-focused Shakespeare season. What I can say is that student and university productions are often more adventurous than one might expect, and they sometimes put clips or programme notes online. If you're planning Twelfth Night for the 2027 session, it may be worth a quick look to see whether either company has shared anything usable in class: a rehearsal photo, a director's note, a short trailer. A comedy about disguise and mistaken identity is a natural companion to the Hamlet opening I mentioned, by the way, since both turn on the question of who someone is when they step out of the dark.

On the Dickens side, there's a review of a production of Great Expectations by Fairy Powered Productions. Again, I have only the title, so I can't tell you what the staging is like or where it's playing. But Great Expectations is also on the 2027 list, and stage adaptations of a long novel are always interesting for what they choose to cut. A useful class question is this: if you had ninety minutes on stage, which scenes of Pip's story would you keep, and who would narrate? That gets at narrative voice, one of the things you love most, and it's a good way to make pupils realise how much of Dickens's novel lives in Pip's retrospective voice rather than in the events themselves. If the review turns out to describe how the company handles that voice, it could be well worth a read.

Now to Margaret Atwood, who appears three times in today's items, though her work sits on the oral themes list rather than the written programme. The most substantial item is a review in Our Theatre Voice of the Canadian premiere of Alias Grace, the stage version of Atwood's novel, which is based on a real nineteenth-century case. The reviewer praises compelling performances and what they call restrained, subtle staging. That detail is worth lingering on. Alias Grace is a novel about a narrator whose account may or may not be reliable, so a staging that is restrained rather than showy seems to suit it. It's not a set text for you, but it speaks to two things your pupils meet on the oral list: Atwood's habit of building fiction from historical record, and the problem of trusting a narrator. If a student has chosen The Handmaid's Tale for the oral, a mention of Atwood's other work set in a real historical past can enrich the conversation about how she handles testimony and silence.

The second Atwood item is from Creative Boom, about the Balbusso Twins returning to The Handmaid's Tale. They are illustrators, and the headline tells us they are going back to the book. I don't have the article's content, so I can't say what they have made or for which edition. But you have a long-standing interest in the links between visual art and writing, and an illustrator's return to a text is exactly that kind of link. Even without details, it's a reminder that The Handmaid's Tale has a strong visual afterlife, in covers, costume and now illustration. For the oral, you could ask pupils to design or choose a cover and justify it with a quotation. The image is the answer to the question, what is this book about, and defending it forces close reading.

The third is from Hotpress, which reports that Margaret Atwood, Sebastian Barry and Louise Kennedy are on the lineup for the Festival of Writing and Ideas in 2027. The text is only a headline, so there are no dates or venue. It's a lineup of three very different voices, though, and Atwood's presence is the connection to your oral list. It's far too early to plan anything, but if details emerge, festival events are often recorded or streamed, and an author talking about her own book is far more persuasive for pupils than any amount of teacher commentary.

There's also an author visit to note. The University Times reports that the Irish novelist Paul Lynch, whose Prophet Song is on the oral themes list, is to visit The Phil, which I take to be the university's debating society, though the item itself doesn't say. No date is given. Still, Prophet Song is one of the newer titles on the list, and any public conversation with Lynch could produce quotable remarks about how he built the novel and why he wrote it as he did. If a recording appears, it could be perfect for a terminale pupil preparing an oral, because it's hard to beat hearing an author explain a choice that the pupil has been wondering about.

That brings me to the Booker Prize, which is the genuinely big literary news. LBC reports that M. John Harrison has won this year's Booker Prize for The End of Everything, described as a dystopian novel. At eighty-one, he becomes the oldest winner, and he is the first science-fiction author to take the prize. I only have the headline facts, so I can't say anything about the book's plot or style, but the milestone speaks for itself. The prize has long been seen as the home of a certain kind of literary realism, and giving it to a writer from science fiction is a real widening of the door. For your classes, there's a nice conversation here about genre. Several of the oral themes titles, among them The Handmaid's Tale, 1984, Never Let Me Go, The Road, Parable of the Sower and Prophet Song, sit somewhere between literary fiction and speculative fiction. Pupils might enjoy debating whether the line between them matters, and whether a prize can change how we see a genre. It's also a charming story in itself: an eighty-one-year-old author taking the biggest prize in English fiction is exactly the kind of good news you like.

Finally, three items that lean towards teaching ideas rather than particular works. Holy Cross Magazine has a piece on teaching the English language through Shakespeare. Only the headline is available, but it sits well with the language work you do in seconde, where Shakespeare can serve as a way into vocabulary, rhythm and word order as much as plot. I'd read it for practical activities. The Wall Street Journal has a piece on the reading list for what it calls the hottest class at Harvard. I've no idea what's on the list, as the text is only a headline, but looking at how a university frames its literature teaching can be a useful source of ideas, or at least a conversation starter with colleagues. And Literary Hub asks the question, what is the best literary TV adaptation of all time? Again, no content to report, but the question is an excellent classroom provocation. You could ask pupils to choose an adaptation of a text they know and defend it: what does a screen version gain, what does it lose, and what does it do with a narrator's voice? That connects neatly with the oral, where adaptation and comparison can give pupils more to say.

A practical word before I finish. Almost all of today's items reached me as headlines only, so none of the productions or articles has been checked for quality or suitability, and I'd treat them as leads to open rather than recommendations. The most promising for you, I think, are the Hamlet photographs, the Alias Grace review and the Booker result, since each gives you something concrete to bring to a lesson.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope something here earns a place in next week's lessons.

There are a few items where all I have is a headline, and I would rather be honest about that than pretend. At Fontanil-Cornillon, there is a Salon des Vins de l'Isère, a regional wine fair. Good morning, Yamuna. It's Tuesday the tenth of November, and today's France news leans heavily towards schools, so I'll start there, then move to language, a couple of stories about the press, a painful chapter of history, and some lighter everyday things.

The big story in education is today's strike. The Local France reports that students and teachers have called for strikes and demonstrations on Tuesday, with a major march expected in Paris. They're pressing the government for more spending on education, after weeks of protests and school closures. Behind that sits the question of the baccalauréat. According to franceinfo, the education minister, Edouard Geffray, has again refused to move the exam dates, despite the pupil protests. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was due to meet lycéen and student representatives on Monday afternoon. The government's line for now is that postponement is ruled out, even though some classes are behind on their programmes after the disruption. Instead it is proposing extra support classes. Franceinfo also looks at the wider debate: whether the bac should be adapted, perhaps by lightening the syllabus or changing the papers. That question will have a particular edge for anyone teaching seconde and première.

The same outlet carries two more human sides of this. One is a report from a headteachers' union, which says about fifty heads of schools have asked for a transfer after the protests. It describes colleagues as discouraged, even traumatised. Some are moving to collèges, some are leaving the profession altogether, and sick leave is rising. The other is from the universities, where two students talk about how the blockades have affected their mental health. One of them says their days no longer resemble much of anything. They're torn between supporting the movement and the isolation and anxiety of worrying whether their year will be validated.

Two other school-related stories are worth knowing. In Brest, franceinfo reports that on the fourth of November two plainclothes police officers, acting under a judicial requisition, collected names, first names and photographs of nearly four thousand five hundred pupils from three lycées. Parents, pupils and unions have called it "fichage", meaning the building of files on pupils, and they are objecting strongly. And a commission on generative artificial intelligence and vulnerability has delivered its report to the Élysée. Its co-chair, Amine Benyamina, warns of what he calls "cognitive debt" and "emotional debt", saying that the use of AI can alter the way we think, reflect and make decisions. It's a phrase your pupils might enjoy arguing about.

On to language, which is a gentler place to be. The Local France has two entries this week. The word of the day is "chouchouter", the verb that grows from "chouchou", meaning a favourite, or a term of endearment. So to chouchouter someone is to pamper them, to treat them as the favourite. It's a lovely sound, and one that could easily turn up in the mouth of a character in a novel. The expression of the day is "avoir les codes", to have the codes. The Local gives only a brief teaser, but the idea is clear enough: knowing the unwritten rules of a place or a group. It's a phrase that would suit a novel of manners just as well as it suits a Parisian dinner party.

Now two stories about the press, both from franceinfo. On Wednesday the eleventh of November, in Paris, there will be a charity football match to mark five hundred days of detention for the French journalist Christophe Gleizes in Algeria. It's organised by Reporters sans frontières and the city hall of Paris, to call for his release. And in Russia, the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta closes its Moscow office today, having already stopped printing in 2022. Franceinfo uses the moment to trace how independent journalism in Russia was silenced or pushed into exile, and how journalists have reinvented their work along the way. It's a sobering piece, but also a story about stubbornness and ingenuity.

There is also a piece of history coming back into view. Five families of harkis, the Algerians who fought alongside the French army during the war of independence, have lodged a complaint about how their relatives' remains were handled in the nineteen-sixties. The case concerns the Saint-Maurice-l'Ardoise camp, in the Gard. The families want the truth about the children who died there. As franceinfo describes it, it is a painful reminder that some stories are still waiting to be properly told, which is often where fiction and history meet.

To end on lighter ground, there is a small bit of good news for anyone who rents a flat. From the twentieth of November, new measures from a rental platform mean that landlords can no longer ask tenants to tidy and clean as much as before. Franceinfo says tenants are pleased. One of them puts it neatly: you can't do everything, either. On the other side of the ledger, The Local France reports that the French tax authority, which has been using aerial photographs to find undeclared swimming pools, will now extend those checks to house extensions, sheds and conservatories. So if you have been thinking about a little garden shed, it may be wise to declare it.

And since the season is coming, The Local also offers a guide to ten of the best Christmas markets in France this year, as towns begin to prepare their streets and squares. The text is brief, but it may be a pleasant thing to browse with a hot drink on a cold evening in Les Adrets.

That's the news for today, Yamuna, and I hope the day treats you like a chouchou.

Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a gentle couple of days for good news, with a prize for a strange and wonderful book, some kindness that took thirty years to arrive, and a surprising number of small creatures being rescued.

Let me begin with books, since they came first. M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything, announced at a ceremony in London. Literary Hub reports that the judges described a book that turns you upside down and raises a wry smile, which is a rather lovely thing to say about any novel, and especially one about the end of the world. The BBC's headline calls it a post-apocalyptic novel, "baffling but brilliant", and I confess I rather like a prize-winner that is allowed to be baffling. That is not a phrase one often hears attached to the Booker. For a writer of Harrison's standing, it is a notable moment, and it suggests the judges were willing to reward something unusual rather than something safe. If you want to read just one piece about it, The Observer has the main analysis, under the title "Why M John Harrison's The End of Everything won the Booker Prize". I would start there, to get a sense of what the book is doing and why the judges fell for it. I only have headlines and summaries from the other two, so I will not pretend to tell you more about the plot. But a post-apocalyptic novel that unsettles its readers and makes them smile at the same time seems well worth your attention, and perhaps a few minutes of discussion with your première students about what we expect a prize-winning novel to look like.

Staying with reading, there is a heartening story from Santa Cruz, California, also from Literary Hub. On Tuesday the sixth of October, during Banned Books Week, three high school seniors organised a sold-out benefit screening of The Librarians, the 2025 documentary. Three teenagers, a documentary about librarians, and a full house. The piece follows the evening itself, watching the film in the company of librarians. It is good to be reminded that the defence of libraries and of reading is not only carried by adults in official roles, and that young people will happily give up an evening, and do a good deal of organising, to stand up for books.

From there I would like to move to stories about people, and the ways they find each other. The first is the one I found most moving. Good News Network tells of a coat that was placed over the shoulders of a Korean schoolgirl after her hanbok, her traditional dress, had been slashed in a racist attack. The coat was given to her by a Japanese teenager, a boy, who stepped in with that small, instinctive act of care. She kept the coat for thirty years. And now, after all that time, it has been returned to the boy who gave it to her, who has finally been found. There is something almost novelistic about the shape of it: a moment of cruelty, a moment of grace, a long silence of three decades, and then a reunion. A coat is such a humble object, and yet it carries the whole story, a bit like the objects that so often carry memory in fiction. It is the sort of thing that would make a very good short story, and it is true.

Another story of unlikely companionship comes from ARTE, and it is on your platform. It is a thirty-two minute documentary from 2021 in the ARTE Regards series, called Agnes et Amir, about living in a shared flat with a centenarian. Agnes Jeschke is a hundred years old and lives in Berlin, and she shares her home with Amir Farahani, a young Iranian refugee. It is a warm portrait of a friendship across a gap of many decades and many worlds, and it is available until the twenty-eighth of April twenty thirty, so there is no hurry. Two strong characters, one who has lived through most of a century and one at the start of a new life in a new country. I suspect you will enjoy listening to the two of them. It might also be a good thing to think about for classes, as a real-life version of the intergenerational friendships that fiction loves so much.

ARTE has a second documentary in the same series that suits you, this one about dance. It is called Lindy hop, se déconnecter et se rencontrer, thirty-one minutes long, made in Germany, and available until the ninth of November twenty twenty-seven. It follows people who have turned away from their screens and towards lindy hop, in Paris and in Pisa, and all the way to Herräng in Sweden. The idea is that dancing together is a way back to presence, to being in a room with other people, touching, listening to the music and to one another. Given how much of our lives now happen through a little glass rectangle, there is something quietly hopeful about people choosing instead to swing out with a stranger. Since you enjoy documentaries about dance, this one looks like a pleasure.

One more human story, and this one is about a young person with real determination. Good News Network reports on a teenager who watched adults misread the cues of his autistic cousin, and decided to do something about it. He taught himself machine learning and built an app called Kora, which helps with interpreting autistic cues. It is free. It now has more than seven hundred users in twelve countries, reached largely through autism therapy centres. What I like here is the order of events. He did not begin with a business plan or an ambition. He began by noticing that someone he loved was not being understood, and then he learned whatever he needed to learn in order to help. It is a lovely example of curiosity put to work out of affection.

Now let me turn to the natural world, where there are three quiet recoveries.

In North Yorkshire, glowworms are shining again in a reserve where they had not been seen for a hundred years. Good News Network tells us that this is thanks to a volunteer, Peter Cooper, who breeds glowworms in his garden shed and releases the larvae into the reserve. A hundred years of darkness, and now a man with a shed and a great deal of patience has put the lights back on. I find this deeply charming. It has the feeling of an English pastoral poem, small and luminous, and it reminds one that conservation sometimes comes down to one person quietly doing a slightly eccentric thing, over and over, until it works.

In Scotland, there is a success on a larger scale, also from Good News Network. Ten years after the country banned industrial scallop dredging, the maerl beds around the Summer Isles are recovering, and fish stocks are thriving. Maerl is a pink seaweed, which grows in beds on the seabed and provides shelter for young fish. The islanders credit their own protection work for the change, and I think that is the heart of the story: a ban on paper matters, but the people who live beside the water kept watch, looked after it, and now have the results to show for it. It is a lovely setting for a good outcome, and a decade is long enough to count as real evidence.

And in Leipzig, scientists have found something rather delightful. Volunteer handlers and their dogs can locate invasive plant species in the wild with about seventy-five per cent accuracy. Invasive plants are a serious threat to biodiversity, and finding them early is half the battle. Dogs, it turns out, are very good at it, and volunteers can work alongside them. It is a practical step, and also a charming one, because it takes something dogs already love to do, which is to follow their noses, and points it at a genuine environmental problem.

That brings me to animals, where this week we have a small parade of rescues and one genuine piece of legislation.

The otter first. Upworthy tells of a man who raised an orphaned otter named Leya, and then released her into the wild. Now he films her swimming out to his kayak for cuddles. Think about that for a moment. She is free, she is a wild animal, she could go anywhere, and she still comes paddling out across the water to see him. It seems to me that this is the best possible ending to a rescue: not a pet kept close, but a wild creature who chooses, now and then, to come back and say hello. The film is said to be tender and very visual, so it should be a pleasure to watch.

Then a more comic tale, also from Upworthy. A traveller was stranded by delays at O'Hare airport in Chicago, and stepped outside for a cigar. A three-week-old stray kitten bolted out of the bushes and adopted him on the spot. He came back inside with a kitten and, as the headline says, a problem. I rather suspect it is not much of a problem, in the end. Three weeks old is tiny, and it is hard not to admire the kitten's judgement in choosing the one person who had nowhere else to be.

And closer to home in spirit, a happy ending from Northampton, via Good News Network. A pet budgie called Luna escaped through a window that Storm Boelo had forced open. She was found a mile from home, in a storm drain, after a passing driver happened to spot her hopping in. A mile is a long way for a small bird, and a storm drain is not where you would hope to find her, so the odds were poor. But somebody was looking in the right place at the right moment, and Luna is home.

Finally, one piece of news that is more than a single heartwarming moment. Positivr reports that the European Union is set to ban tail docking, la caudectomie, for all companion animals from twenty twenty-eight. This is the cosmetic and surgical practice of cutting the tails of dogs, and it has been going on for centuries. The decision is reported as settled, which means it is not merely a proposal waiting to be debated. For animal welfare, it is a concrete step, and it is one of those changes which, once made, will quickly seem obvious.

So that is the news: a baffling and brilliant prize-winner, a coat returned after thirty years, glowworms back in Yorkshire, and a budgie safe at home. I hope there is a cup of something warm within reach, and perhaps a dog or an otter somewhere in your day.

Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Tuesday. It's the tenth of November, and the literary news is rather good today.

It follows people who put down their screens and take up dancing, from Paris and Pisa to Herräng in Sweden. It's a warm portrait of dance as a way back to being present.

Now for some good news. In North Yorkshire, a volunteer called Peter Cooper breeds glowworms in his garden shed. He releases the larvae into a nature reserve where the insects hadn't been seen for a hundred years, so they are shining there again. And in Scotland, ten years after industrial scallop dredging was banned, the maerl beds of the Summer Isles are recovering, a pink seaweed that shelters young fish, and fish stocks are thriving. The islanders credit their own protection work, which is a lovely thing to hear.

A word for the terminale classes ahead. Our Theatre Voice reviews the Canadian premiere of Alias Grace, the stage version of Margaret Atwood's novel, based on a real nineteenth-century case. The reviewer praises the compelling performances and the restrained, subtle staging. If you're thinking about Atwood and her historical setting, it could make a nice thing to bring to class.

On language, The Local France has two for you. The word of the day is chouchouter, the verb from chouchou, a favourite or a term of endearment, and the article explains its several uses. It's a good word to spoil yourself with today. The expression of the day is avoir les codes, to have the codes, though all I have is a short teaser, so I can't say more about it.

Finally, closer to home. At Hexagone Scène nationale in Meylan, on the ninth of December at a quarter past two in the afternoon, Collectif Mind The Gap presents J'étais parti·e, pardon, a show about how we might change worlds. It's for ages eight and up, runs fifty-five minutes, and has three more dates if that one doesn't suit. And the Salon des Vins de l'Isère, a regional wine fair, is being held at Fontanil-Cornillon. I only have the headline, with no dates, so it's worth a quick look before you go.

That's the Daily Yam for today. I hope the mountain light is kind to you in Les Adrets, and that you find a lovely sentence or two along the way.
